def lex_min_binary_matrix(row_sums, col_sums):
    """Construct the lexicographically smallest 0/1 matrix with given margins.

    Given row_sums (a list of m integers) and col_sums (a list of n
    integers), consider all m-by-n matrices with entries in {0, 1} such that
    row i contains exactly row_sums[i] ones and column j contains exactly
    col_sums[j] ones.  Among all such matrices, return the one whose
    row-major concatenation (row 0 read left to right, then row 1, and so
    on) is lexicographically smallest as a string of '0'/'1' characters.
    That matrix is unique, so there are no ties to break.

    Input domain: 1 <= m, n <= 40, and every element of row_sums and
    col_sums is an integer with 0 <= value <= 40 (a value may exceed the
    other dimension, in which case no valid matrix exists).

    Output: a list of m strings, each of length n over the characters '0'
    and '1' -- the rows of the matrix, top to bottom.  If no matrix has the
    given margins, return [] (the empty list).

    Note the search space holds up to 2**1600 matrices, so enumeration is
    hopeless, and a greedy that simply pushes ones rightward in each row
    without an exact completability test returns wrong answers.

    >>> lex_min_binary_matrix([2, 1], [1, 1, 1])
    ['011', '100']
    >>> lex_min_binary_matrix([1, 2], [2, 1, 0])
    ['100', '110']
    >>> lex_min_binary_matrix([2], [2, 0])
    []
    """
